claim: In 2019, 6,292 respondents participated in the national postdoc survey.
source: In 2019, 6,292 respondents participated in our national postdoc survey, of which 5,929 identified as postdocs working in the US (we only analyzed responses from US-based postdocs).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of respondents in the 2019 survey.

claim: 5,929 respondents identified as postdocs working in the US in the 2019 survey.
source: In 2019, 6,292 respondents participated in our national postdoc survey, of which 5,929 identified as postdocs working in the US (we only analyzed responses from US-based postdocs).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of US-based postdocs in the 2019 survey.

claim: In October 2020, 1,942 of the 6,292 respondents who participated in the 2019 survey completed a follow-up survey.
source: In October of 2020, 1,942 of the 6,292 respondents who participated in the 2019 survey, completed a follow-up survey assessing the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of respondents in the 2020 follow-up survey.

claim: 1,722 (89%) of the 2020 survey respondents were still in a postdoctoral position at a US institution.
source: Of these, 1,722 (89%) were still in a postdoctoral position at a US institution.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number and percentage of respondents still in postdoctoral positions.

claim: There were more self-identified female respondents in the pandemic survey (61%) compared to the pre-pandemic survey (58%).
source: There were slightly more responses from individuals who identified as female (61% vs 58%) and non-binary/third gender (0.9% vs 0.4%), and fewer self-identified males (38% vs 42%) in the pandemic survey compared to the pre-pandemic survey (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1A shows the gender distribution comparison.

claim: There were more self-identified non-binary/third gender respondents in the pandemic survey (0.9%) compared to the pre-pandemic survey (0.4%).
source: There were slightly more responses from individuals who identified as female (61% vs 58%) and non-binary/third gender (0.9% vs 0.4%), and fewer self-identified males (38% vs 42%) in the pandemic survey compared to the pre-pandemic survey (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1A shows the gender distribution comparison.

claim: There were fewer self-identified male respondents in the pandemic survey (38%) compared to the pre-pandemic survey (42%).
source: There were slightly more responses from individuals who identified as female (61% vs 58%) and non-binary/third gender (0.9% vs 0.4%), and fewer self-identified males (38% vs 42%) in the pandemic survey compared to the pre-pandemic survey (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1A shows the gender distribution comparison.

claim: The gender distribution difference between pre-pandemic and pandemic surveys was statistically significant (Chi-squared test, P=0.0023, χ2=12.2).
source: (A) More self-identified female and third gender/non-binary and fewer self-identified male respondents completed the pandemic survey (n=1,698) compared to the pre-pandemic survey (Chi-squared test, P=0.0023, χ2=12.2; n=5,805).
evidence: Figure 1 legend provides statistical test results for gender distribution differences.

claim: The majority of respondents were white in both the pre-pandemic and pandemic surveys.
source: (B) The majority of respondents were white in both the pre-pandemic (n=5,649) and pandemic surveys (n=1,673), with an increase in white and a decrease in Asian respondents in the pandemic survey compared to the pre-pandemic survey (Chi-squared test, P=0.0024, χ2=12.1).
evidence: Figure 1 legend states the racial composition of respondents.

claim: There was an increase in white respondents and a decrease in Asian respondents in the pandemic survey compared to the pre-pandemic survey.
source: Race and ethnicity varied between the pre-pandemic and pandemic survey respondents, with a 4% increase in the proportion of respondents who identify as white, and a corresponding 4% decrease in the respondents who identify as Asian; however, no differences were observed between the proportion of respondents from underrepresented minority backgrounds (URMs; 13% in both surveys; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage changes and Figure 1B shows the racial distribution comparison.

claim: No differences were observed between the proportion of respondents from underrepresented minority backgrounds (URMs; 13% in both surveys).
source: Race and ethnicity varied between the pre-pandemic and pandemic survey respondents, with a 4% increase in the proportion of respondents who identify as white, and a corresponding 4% decrease in the respondents who identify as Asian; however, no differences were observed between the proportion of respondents from underrepresented minority backgrounds (URMs; 13% in both surveys; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states that URM representation remained constant at 13% in both surveys.

claim: The number of respondents who were US citizens or permanent residents increased from 53% (pre-pandemic survey) to 57% (pandemic survey).
source: The number of respondents who were US citizens or permanent residents (referred to as US citizens/PR throughout this manuscript) increased from 53% (pre-pandemic survey) to 57% (pandemic survey).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the percentages of US citizens/PR in both surveys.

claim: There was a corresponding decrease in international respondents from 47% (pre-pandemic) to 43% (pandemic) who were working in the US on temporary visas.
source: There was a corresponding decrease in international respondents (47% pre-pandemic vs. 43% pandemic) who were working in the US on temporary visas (J1, H1B, TN, F1, F1-OTP, E3 visas; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1C shows the citizenship status comparison.

claim: The age of the pandemic respondents was slightly higher than the pre-pandemic respondents.
source: Given that we conducted the pandemic survey within a sub-population of those in the pre-pandemic survey at a later date, the age of the pandemic respondents was slightly higher than the pre-pandemic respondents, and as expected, they were more advanced in their postdoc (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The manuscript states the age difference and Figure 1D shows the age distribution comparison.

claim: Pandemic respondents were more advanced in their postdoc compared to pre-pandemic respondents.
source: Given that we conducted the pandemic survey within a sub-population of those in the pre-pandemic survey at a later date, the age of the pandemic respondents was slightly higher than the pre-pandemic respondents, and as expected, they were more advanced in their postdoc (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The manuscript states the advancement difference and Figure 1E shows the years of postdoc experience comparison.

claim: There was a significant decrease in respondents in the field of medicine (13% pre-pandemic and 9% pandemic).
source: There was a significant decrease in respondents in the field of medicine (13% pre-pandemic and 9% pandemic), while there was no significant change in the representation of any other field (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1F shows the field distribution comparison.

claim: There was a significant increase in access to a PDO (65.6% pre-pandemic vs 70% pandemic), which was mainly due to increased awareness.
source: Lastly, there was a significant increase in access to a PDO (65.6% pre-pandemic vs 70% pandemic), which was mainly due to increased awareness, but no differences in access to a PDA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F shows the PDO access comparison.

claim: Postdocs' main stressors during the pandemic were a combination of work, family, and emotional burdens (such as uncertainty, isolation, fear, and anxiety).
source: In an open-ended question inquiring about main stressors during the pandemic, postdocs indicated that their main stressors were a combination of work, family, and emotional burdens (such as uncertainty, isolation, fear, and anxiety) as shown by the word cloud analysis of the responses (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The manuscript states the main stressors and Figure 2A-B shows the word cloud analysis.

claim: Most postdocs indicated that they were completely or mostly satisfied with their institution's response to COVID-19 (59%).
source: Most postdocs indicated that they were completely or mostly satisfied with their institution's response to COVID-19 (59%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 2C shows the satisfaction distribution.

claim: Postdocs with access to a PDO were significantly more satisfied with their institution's response to COVID-19 than those who did not have a PDO.
source: In particular, postdocs with access to a PDO were significantly more satisfied than those who did not (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript states the relationship and Figure 2D shows the satisfaction comparison by PDO access.

claim: Satisfaction with the institution's response to COVID-19 was higher in postdocs that had access to a PDO compared to those who did not have a PDO (multivariate ordinal logistic regression P=0.0021, Odds Ratio (OR)=1.81 [95% Confidence Interval (CI); 1.24–2.65]).
source: (D) Satisfaction with the institution's response to COVID-19 was higher in postdocs that had access to a PDO compared to the ones that did not have a PDO at their institution (multivariate ordinal logistic regression P=0.0021, Odds Ratio (OR)=1.81 [95% Confidence Interval (CI); 1.24–2.65]; n=1,613) or those unaware whether their institution had a PDO (multivariate ordinal logistic regression P=0.044, OR=1.24 [95% CI; 1.01–1.53]; n=1,700).
evidence: Figure 2 legend provides statistical test results for satisfaction differences by PDO access.

claim: There were no differences in satisfaction with their institution's response between those with or without access to a PDA.
source: On the other hand, there were no differences in satisfaction with their institution's response between those with or without access to a PDA (Figure 2D), or with respect to gender, citizenship status, race and ethnicity, or identity (multivariate ordinal logistic regression, P>0.05, data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript states no significant differences and Figure 2D shows the satisfaction comparison by PDA access.

claim: 4% of postdocs indicated they were completely unsatisfied with their institution's response to COVID-19.
source: Notably, there was also a non-negligible portion (4%) of postdocs who indicated they were completely unsatisfied with their institution's response to COVID-19, with one respondent commenting, "... my institution did almost NOTHING to ensure that faculty and staff can be safely back at work".
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage of completely unsatisfied respondents.

claim: 64% of postdocs indicated that all of their basic needs were met during the pandemic.
source: Although the majority of postdocs indicated that all of their basic needs were met during the pandemic (64%), a substantial portion (36%) indicated that their needs concerning mental health (21%), childcare (11%), healthcare (7%) and/or food (2%) were unmet (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 2E shows the basic needs distribution.

claim: 36% of postdocs indicated that their needs concerning mental health (21%), childcare (11%), healthcare (7%) and/or food (2%) were unmet during the pandemic.
source: Although the majority of postdocs indicated that all of their basic needs were met during the pandemic (64%), a substantial portion (36%) indicated that their needs concerning mental health (21%), childcare (11%), healthcare (7%) and/or food (2%) were unmet (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages of unmet needs and Figure 2E shows the distribution.

claim: 3% of postdocs mentioned other unmet needs including the inability to pay bills or exercise, and loss of access to transportation, work safety, human connections, or loss of salary, retirement benefits, or annual raise.
source: Additionally, 3% of postdocs mentioned other unmet needs in their responses, including the inability to pay bills or exercise, and loss of access to transportation, work safety, human connections, or loss of salary, retirement benefits, or annual raise.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and lists the types of other unmet needs.

claim: Postdocs who had access to a PDA or PDO were more likely to have their basic needs met (65% PDA; 66% PDO) than those who did not (50% PDA; 56% PDO).
source: Postdocs who had access to a PDA or PDO (although not statistically significant for the latter) were more likely to have their basic needs met (65% PDA; 66% PDO) than those who did not (50% PDA; 56% PDO; Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 2F shows the basic needs comparison by PDA/PDO access.

claim: Postdocs with access to a PDO or a PDA were less likely to have their mental health needs unmet (PDO: 32% (no) vs. 19% (yes); PDA: 37% (no) vs. 20% (yes)).
source: Furthermore, postdocs with access to a PDO or a PDA were less likely to have their mental health needs unmet (PDO: 32% (no) vs. 19% (yes); PDA: 37% (no) vs. 20% (yes)); no differences were observed between those not aware and aware of a PDA or PDO at their institution (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 2F shows the mental health needs comparison by PDA/PDO access.

claim: Having access to a PDO or a PDA significantly impacted having mental health needs met (multivariate logistic regression, No PDO P=0.02, OR=0.57 [95% CI; 0.35–0.91]; No PDA P=0.026, OR=0.52 [95% CI; 0.29–0.93]).
source: (F) Having access to a PDO or a PDA significantly impacted having mental health needs met (multivariate logistic regression, No PDO P=0.02, OR=0.57 [95% CI; 0.35–0.91]; No PDA P=0.026, OR=0.52 [95% CI; 0.29–0.93]; n=1,614).
evidence: Figure 2 legend provides statistical test results for mental health needs by PDA/PDO access.

claim: Postdocs who identified as Asian were less likely to have their health care (12% vs 5%) or food (5% vs 1%) basic needs met compared to white respondents.
source: Postdocs who identified as Asian – the majority of whom were international (76%) – were more likely than white postdocs to report unmet needs with respect to health care (12% vs 6%) or food (6% vs 1%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows the basic needs comparison by race/ethnicity.

claim: Postdocs who identified as LGBTQ reported an increase in food (5% vs 2%) and mental health (30% vs 20%) needs unmet compared to postdocs who did not identify as LGBTQ.
source: Postdocs who identified as LGBTQ reported an increase in food (5% vs 2%) and mental health (30% vs 20%) needs unmet compared to postdocs who did not identify as LGBTQ. (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows the basic needs comparison by LGBTQ status.

claim: Postdocs who reported having a disability were less likely to have their mental health basic needs met (40% vs 20%) compared to postdocs without disabilities.
source: The latter was also observed in postdocs with disabilities compared to postdocs without disabilities (40% vs 20%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows the mental health needs comparison by disability status.

claim: In the pre-pandemic survey, 20% of postdocs answered that they had children.
source: While we did not directly inquire whether respondents in the pandemic survey had children (in the pre-pandemic survey, 20% of postdocs answered that they had children), 10% of respondents mentioned in comments that ensuring their children had proper care was a major stressor and led to severe work disruptions.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage of postdocs with children in the pre-pandemic survey.

claim: 10% of respondents mentioned in comments that ensuring their children had proper care was a major stressor and led to severe work disruptions.
source: While we did not directly inquire whether respondents in the pandemic survey had children (in the pre-pandemic survey, 20% of postdocs answered that they had children), 10% of respondents mentioned in comments that ensuring their children had proper care was a major stressor and led to severe work disruptions.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage of respondents who mentioned childcare as a stressor.

claim: 68% of comments about childcare stressors were from female respondents and 32% from males, suggesting a greater burden of childcare for female postdocs.
source: Additionally, 68% of these comments were from female respondents and 32% from males, suggesting a greater burden of childcare for female postdocs.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and infers a greater burden on female postdocs.

claim: Childcare was the 5th most frequently mentioned stressor.
source: Overall, childcare was the 5th most frequently mentioned stressor (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The manuscript states the ranking and Figure 2A-B shows the word cloud analysis.

claim: More international postdocs (vs. US citizens/PR) reported having food needs unmet (4% vs 1%).
source: When we focused on residency status, we saw that more international postdocs (vs. US citizens/PR) reported having food needs unmet (4% vs 1%), while US citizens/PR (vs. international postdocs) reported more difficulty in obtaining childcare (13% vs 9%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 3A shows the basic needs comparison by citizenship status.

claim: US citizens/PR (vs. international postdocs) reported more difficulty in obtaining childcare (13% vs 9%).
source: When we focused on residency status, we saw that more international postdocs (vs. US citizens/PR) reported having food needs unmet (4% vs 1%), while US citizens/PR (vs. international postdocs) reported more difficulty in obtaining childcare (13% vs 9%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 3A shows the basic needs comparison by citizenship status.

claim: The majority of international postdocs (84%) reported apprehension about immigration or visas due to recent policy changes in the US.
source: The majority of international postdocs reported apprehension about immigration or visas either due to recent policy changes in the US (84%) or in general (11%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 3B shows the immigration concerns distribution.

claim: 11% of international postdocs reported apprehension about immigration or visas in general (not due to recent policy changes).
source: The majority of international postdocs reported apprehension about immigration or visas either due to recent policy changes in the US (84%) or in general (11%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 3B shows the immigration concerns distribution.

claim: The primary immigration concerns noted by international postdocs were traveling (75%), US immigration policy changes (69%), and travel bans (68%).
source: The primary concerns noted were traveling (75%), US immigration policy changes (69%), and travel bans (68%) (Figure 3C, Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 3C shows the immigration concerns distribution.

claim: More international females than males were worried about immigration issues (89% vs 78%).
source: Furthermore, more international females than males were worried about immigration issues (89% vs 78%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A); specifically, travel (80% vs 70%), delays in visa renewal (65% vs 56%), and travel bans (72% vs 62%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows the immigration concerns comparison by gender.

claim: 76% of respondents stated that the COVID-19 pandemic had impacted their mental health.
source: Overall, 76% of respondents stated that the COVID-19 pandemic had impacted their mental health, with 32% stating that it had a high or very high impact (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 4A shows the mental health impact distribution.

claim: 32% of respondents stated that the COVID-19 pandemic had a high or very high impact on their mental health.
source: Overall, 76% of respondents stated that the COVID-19 pandemic had impacted their mental health, with 32% stating that it had a high or very high impact (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 4A shows the mental health impact distribution.

source: However, certain groups reported more of an impact than others; females reported a greater impact than males (80% vs 68%); white and URM postdocs reported more of an impact than Asian postdocs (78% and 80% vs 68%); members of the LGBTQ community (83% vs 75%) and postdocs with disabilities (88% vs 76%) reported more of an impact than postdocs not identifying with these groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 4B shows the mental health impact comparison by gender.

claim: White and URM postdocs reported more of an impact on mental health than Asian postdocs (78% and 80% vs 68%).
source: However, certain groups reported more of an impact than others; females reported a greater impact than males (80% vs 68%); white and URM postdocs reported more of an impact than Asian postdocs (78% and 80% vs 68%); members of the LGBTQ community (83% vs 75%) and postdocs with disabilities (88% vs 76%) reported more of an impact than postdocs not identifying with these groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 4B shows the mental health impact comparison by race/ethnicity.

claim: Members of the LGBTQ community reported more of an impact on mental health (83% vs 75%) than postdocs not identifying with this group.
source: However, certain groups reported more of an impact than others; females reported a greater impact than males (80% vs 68%); white and URM postdocs reported more of an impact than Asian postdocs (78% and 80% vs 68%); members of the LGBTQ community (83% vs 75%) and postdocs with disabilities (88% vs 76%) reported more of an impact than postdocs not identifying with these groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 4B shows the mental health impact comparison by LGBTQ status.

claim: Postdocs with disabilities reported more of an impact on mental health (88% vs 76%) than postdocs without disabilities.
source: However, certain groups reported more of an impact than others; females reported a greater impact than males (80% vs 68%); white and URM postdocs reported more of an impact than Asian postdocs (78% and 80% vs 68%); members of the LGBTQ community (83% vs 75%) and postdocs with disabilities (88% vs 76%) reported more of an impact than postdocs not identifying with these groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 4B shows the mental health impact comparison by disability status.

claim: Access to institutional mental health resources rose by 15% during the pandemic.
source: Parallel to this impact on mental health, access to institutional mental health resources rose by 15% (Figure 5A), which appears to be linked to an increase in awareness, although only 17% of postdocs indicated use of these resources.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage increase and Figure 5A shows the access comparison.

claim: Only 17% of postdocs indicated use of institutional mental health resources.
source: Parallel to this impact on mental health, access to institutional mental health resources rose by 15% (Figure 5A), which appears to be linked to an increase in awareness, although only 17% of postdocs indicated use of these resources.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage of postdocs who used mental health resources.

claim: Female postdocs reported higher usage of mental health resources compared to male postdocs (21% vs 10%).
source: Female postdocs reported higher usage of these resources compared to male postdocs (21% vs 10%; Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 4B shows the mental health resource usage comparison by gender.

claim: Postdocs without access to, or who were unaware of, institutional mental health resources were more likely to have their mental health impacted by COVID-19 than postdocs with access to those resources.
source: Notably, postdocs without access to, or who were unaware of, institutional mental health resources were more likely to have their mental health impacted by COVID-19 than postdocs with access to those resources (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript states the relationship and Figure 5B shows the mental health impact comparison by access to mental health resources.

claim: Postdocs were more likely to have their mental health needs met if their institution provided mental health resources (84%) than if their institution either did not provide them (42%) or if they were unaware of these resources at their institution (68%).
source: Indeed, postdocs were more likely to have their mental health needs met if their institution provided these resources (84%) than if their institution either did not provide them (42%) or if they were unaware of these resources at their institution (68%, Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 5C shows the mental health needs comparison by access to mental health resources.

claim: Postdocs at institutions that provided mental health resources were more likely to have all their basic needs met (69%) compared to those without (35%) or unaware of these resources (50%).
source: Postdocs at institutions that provided mental health resources were also more likely to have all their basic needs met (69%) compared to those without (35%) or unaware of these resources (50%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 5D shows the basic needs comparison by access to mental health resources.

claim: Access to a PDA and/or a PDO increased the likelihood of mental health needs being met.
source: As previously indicated (Figure 2F), access to a PDA and/or a PDO also increased the likelihood of mental health needs being met.
evidence: The manuscript states the relationship between PDA/PDO access and mental health needs being met.

claim: A larger proportion of postdocs with access to a PDO/PDA had access to mental health resources (82% and 80%) compared to those that did not (59% and 61%) or were unaware (66% and 60%).
source: This trend may be due in part to a larger proportion of postdocs with access to a PDO/PDA also having access to mental health resources (82% and 80%) compared to those that did not (59% and 61%) or were unaware (66% and 60%) (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 5E-F shows the mental health resource access comparison by PDA/PDO access.

claim: Postdocs with a PDO/PDA were more likely to use their institution's mental health resources (19% and 18%) compared to those that did not have access (9% and 11%) or were unaware of these resources (13% and 9%).
source: Postdocs with a PDO/PDA were also more likely to use their institution's mental health resources (19% and 18%) compared to those that did not have access (9% and 11%) or were unaware of these resources (13% and 9%, Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 5E-F shows the mental health resource usage comparison by PDA/PDO access.

claim: A smaller proportion of postdocs were currently looking for positions during the pandemic (56%) compared to pre-pandemic (64%).
source: Even though the postdocs were older and had more years of experience when re-surveyed (Figure 1D–E), a smaller proportion were currently looking for positions (64% pre-pandemic, 56% during the pandemic), with 11% of postdocs specifically delaying their job search because of the pandemic (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 6A shows the job search comparison.

claim: 11% of postdocs specifically delayed their job search because of the pandemic.
source: Even though the postdocs were older and had more years of experience when re-surveyed (Figure 1D–E), a smaller proportion were currently looking for positions (64% pre-pandemic, 56% during the pandemic), with 11% of postdocs specifically delaying their job search because of the pandemic (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 6A shows the job search status.

claim: Postdocs were less confident in achieving their career goals during the pandemic (68% said they were very confident to somewhat confident) compared to before the pandemic (76%).
source: In addition, postdocs were less confident in achieving their career goals than before the pandemic (Figure 6B, 76% said they were very confident to somewhat confident pre-pandemic compared to 68% during the pandemic), which may be contributing to the observed decline in those actively pursuing new positions (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 6B shows the confidence comparison.

claim: More postdocs were undecided about their future careers during the pandemic (12%) than before the pandemic (9%).
source: Furthermore, more postdocs were undecided about their future careers than before the pandemic (9%–12%) (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 6C shows the career plans comparison.

source: Overall, 34% of postdocs reported changing their career plans during the pandemic, with 23% of respondents indicating that COVID-19 was the direct cause of their change (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 6D shows the career plan changes.

claim: 23% of respondents indicated that COVID-19 was the direct cause of their career plan change.
source: Overall, 34% of postdocs reported changing their career plans during the pandemic, with 23% of respondents indicating that COVID-19 was the direct cause of their change (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 6D shows the career plan changes.

source: Of those postdocs who indicated a change in career plans (both due and not due to the pandemic), the main reasons cited were: (i) difficulty in obtaining the desired position (77%), (ii) insufficient job security (52%), and (iii) balancing family and career (50%) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 6E shows the reasons for career plan changes.

claim: The majority of postdocs surveyed (81%) reported a change in their perception of the job market.

claim: More US citizens/PR than international postdocs (85% vs 74%) reported a change in perception of the job market.
source: The majority of postdocs surveyed also reported a change in their perception of the job market (81%) (Figure 6F), with more US citizens/PR than international postdocs (85% vs 74%, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) reporting a change in perception.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D shows the job market perception comparison by citizenship status.

claim: The majority of the respondents viewed the current academic job market as poor (66%) or fair (26%) during the pandemic.

evidence: The manuscript states the percentages of job market perception during the pandemic.

claim: In the pre-pandemic survey, fewer postdocs viewed the academic job market as poor (44%) and more viewed it as fair (33%).
source: Overall, the majority of the respondents viewed the current academic job market as poor (66%) or fair (26%), which is a significant change compared to the pre-pandemic survey, where fewer postdocs viewed the market as poor (44%) and more viewed it as fair (33%).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentages of job market perception before the pandemic.

evidence: The manuscript states the percentages of job market perception for non-academic vs academic careers.

source: Of those who responded to the second survey, 11% (219/1,941) were no longer postdocs, with 14% indicating that this career transition was a consequence of the pandemic (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage and Figure 7A shows the career transition status.

claim: Nearly 8% of postdocs who made career transitions were unemployed.
